step1_summary: Chief complaint: "Not feeling very well" for 4–5 days with cough and cold-type symptoms.

Symptoms: • Onset Saturday (≈5 days). • Cough mainly dry, worse in a.m., admits to “mucky phlegm” occasionally. • Runny nose/sniffles. • Sore throat (also shouts at football). • Mild ear dullness. • Shortness of breath (“not good”) without chest pain. • Subjective fever/rigors—night sweats, blanket on/off; no temperature taken. • 1 day of diarrhoea early on, now resolved. • General myalgias/joint stiffness. • Appetite preserved; keeping up fluids; no vomiting.
Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, overweight/obese.
Medications: Metformin, Lisinopril; intermittent aspirin.  Allergies: none known.
Social history: Lives with wife, adult children moved out. Works in steel-parts factory. Alcohol ≈9 pints beer/week. Occasional smoker; currently switching to vaping.
Vital signs / exam: Telephone visit—no vitals or physical exam documented.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute dyspnoea and cough could represent PE, especially in overweight, smoker, but viral prodrome makes it less likely.
Congestive heart failure exacerbation: New dyspnoea and cough; comorbid HTN/DM are risk factors.
I: Influenza / COVID-19 / other viral URTI: Classic triad of cough, myalgias, feverishness over few days.
Community-acquired pneumonia (bacterial): Cough with purulent sputum, fevers, dyspnoea; DM is a risk factor.
Acute bronchitis (viral/bacterial): Sub-acute cough often following URTI, may have low-grade fever and sputum.
N: Lung malignancy: Cough and weight-loss/haemoptysis absent; acute onset argues against but considered.
D: COPD or degenerative airways disease: Smoker with chronic cough possibility, though onset acute.
Iron-deficiency or other anaemia: Could contribute to tiredness/SOB.
I2: Alcohol excess irritation of airway but intake moderate.
C: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency–related lung disease: Unlikely given age/onset but remotely possible.
A: Allergic rhinitis/pharyngitis: Runny nose, throat irritation, but systemic symptoms less typical.
T: Chest wall strain from shouting or coughing—not primary diagnosis.
E: Diabetic ketoacidosis / metabolic derangement: Infection trigger possible; no polyuria/polydipsia reported.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / Influenza-like illness (include COVID-19)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most common cause of abrupt onset cough, rhinorrhoea, sore throat, myalgias and subjective fever over 4–5 days in otherwise healthy adult during community exposure; diarrhoea also seen with many respiratory viruses (esp. COVID).
Progressive cough now with ‘mucky’ sputum, feverishness and increasing dyspnoea; diabetic middle-aged male is higher risk for bacterial LRTI.
Sub-acute (≤3 weeks) cough—initially viral—with or without minimal sputum, mild fever and limited systemic toxicity; fits many features and often overlaps with viral URI.
Chronic dry cough is a classic side-effect; however sudden onset with systemic symptoms and sputum make this less plausible.
Dyspnoea and cough in patient with HTN/DM could signal new HF, but absence of orthopnoea, peripheral oedema or cardiac history plus presence of URI symptoms argue against.

step4_evidence.diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / Influenza-like illness (incl. COVID-19)
supporting_evidence: Self-limited diarrhoea (seen in many viral illnesses).
No focal chest pain; largely systemic/upper airway picture.
opposing_evidence: Shortness of breath described as ‘not good’ raises concern for lower airway involvement.
Admits to some ‘mucky’ sputum which can suggest bacterial process.

supporting_evidence: Risk factors: Type 2 DM, smoker, male age 50.
opposing_evidence: No objective fever, tachypnoea, or abnormal lung exam documented.
Runny nose and sore throat more typical of URI.

supporting_evidence: Often presents with minimal sputum and mild fever.
Shortness of breath common but usually mild; physical exam often benign (not available here).
opposing_evidence: Presence of systemic myalgias/rigors can be more in keeping with influenza or pneumonia.
Physician felt borderline about antibiotics, implying possible bacterial process.

supporting_evidence: Dry, non-productive cough is classic side-effect.
opposing_evidence: Cough only present 5 days (ACE cough usually chronic).
Associated fever, rhinorrhoea, sore throat not explained.

supporting_evidence: Dyspnoea and cough; comorbid HTN/DM and overweight status predispose.
opposing_evidence: Abrupt viral-type prodrome, fever, upper-respiratory symptoms not typical for HF.
No orthopnoea, PND, peripheral oedema, or cardiac history.
